briefs.bs-neonatal-sepsis:
Fever and Sepsis in the Newborn

neonatal sepsis, its mimics and the febrile infant to 60 days · a laboratory value decides when the temperature does not; every reliable negative closes a sourceIs a laboratory value the only sign, and which source remains?

DiagnosisWorkup by agePracticeManagement
Bottom line

Fever is unreliable in the first month: neonates with sepsis may be afebrile or hypothermic, so without fever the laboratory results decide. With fever, the age band sets the workup.

  • Early-onset sepsis: onset within 72 hours; organisms from the maternal genital tract: group B Streptococcus (GBS), Escherichia coli and Listeria.
  • Late-onset sepsis: onset 72 hours to 90 days; nosocomial organisms join: coagulase-negative staphylococci, Staphylococcus aureus, and Candida in very low birth weight (VLBW) infants.
  • Leukopenia: the total white blood cell count (WBC) predicts early-onset sepsis poorly, but a low count in a neonate with these signs is sepsis until proven otherwise; it reflects marrow depletion by overwhelming infection and is more ominous than leukocytosis.
  • Paradoxical irritability: quiet when undisturbed, crying on being picked up or moved, because handling stretches inflamed meninges: the meningeal sign of infancy.
  • Neonatal empiric coverage: ampicillin plus gentamicin: ampicillin for GBS and Listeria (cephalosporins miss Listeria), gentamicin for gram-negative organisms (cefotaxime may be added or substituted if gram-negative meningitis is suspected); ampicillin plus cefotaxime when meningitis is strongly suspected or confirmed; ceftriaxone is avoided.

Workup by age
Practice
  1. 3-day-old girl born at term is irritable and refusing feeds No maternal drug use or thyroid disease no tremor, sneezing or high-pitched cry T 37.0 °C (normothermic) · HR 180/min · white blood cells 3,000/mm³ · glucose normal → Ampicillin and gentamicin → leukopenia is the one value that separates sepsis from the behavioral mimics: it reflects marrow depletion by overwhelming infection and is more ominous than leukocytosis. Ampicillin covers group B Streptococcus and Listeria, and gentamicin the gram-negative organisms. Intravenous dextrose answers a low glucose, and morphine answers neonatal abstinence, which brings tremor with a normal count. The total white cell count predicts early-onset sepsis poorly on its own, but here it is the one abnormal value. Leukopenia is also a herpes simplex virus risk feature, so acyclovir may be considered ⚠︎
  2. 7-month-old boy has fever and cries violently when picked up lies quietly when left undisturbed Three loose stools today; no cough or rhinorrhea T 39.5 °C · white blood cells 16,000/mm³ with 83% neutrophils · urine dipstick negative, specific gravity 1.030 → Lumbar puncture for Gram stain and culture → crying on being handled with calm when undisturbed is paradoxical irritability, the meningeal sign of infancy. No cough or rhinorrhea closes the respiratory branch; a negative dipstick in concentrated urine closes the urinary branch. Three loose stools are a nonspecific systemic response and do not explain the paradoxical irritability, and paroxysmal crying with a mass would earn the ultrasound
  3. 2-day-old boy is jittery with a high-pitched cry Mother used heroin throughout the pregnancy frequent sneezing hyperactive Moro reflex T 37.1 °C · HR 164/min · white blood cells 12,000/mm³ · glucose normal → Neonatal abstinence syndrome → maternal opioid use with onset at 24 to 72 hours, a high-pitched cry, tremor, sneezing and a hyperactive Moro reflex with a normal white cell count; supportive care, considering morphine if severe. A normal glucose excludes hypoglycemia, and a normal count with a clear drug history argues against sepsis
  4. 9-month-old boy has episodes of crying with his legs drawn up Calm between episodes, but now lethargic Episodes began 6 hours ago and recur every 20 minutes sausage-shaped right upper quadrant mass T 37.6 °C · HR 150/min → Abdominal ultrasound → paroxysmal crying with pain-free intervals and a sausage mass at 6 to 36 months: the ultrasound shows a target sign. Paroxysmal crying with calm intervals is the mirror of the constant paradoxical irritability that earns a lumbar puncture
  5. 1-day-old girl is jittery and lethargic Mother had gestational diabetes large for gestational age Born at 39 weeks by cesarean delivery; Apgar scores 8 and 9 T 36.8 °C · HR 150/min · glucose 28 mg/dL → Intravenous dextrose infusion → an infant of a diabetic mother with jitteriness, lethargy and a glucose below 40 to 45 mg/dL is symptomatic hypoglycemia, treated with intravenous dextrose. Antibiotics answer leukopenia, not a low glucose, and observation leaves a symptomatic infant untreated
  6. 8-month-old girl has fever with no localizing findings No cough, rhinorrhea or diarrhea Immunizations are up to date; fever began 2 days ago catheterized urine dipstick positive for leukocyte esterase T 39.2 °C · HR 160/min → Urine culture and empiric antibiotics → the commonest serious bacterial infection in febrile infants: a positive dipstick sends the urine for culture and starts antibiotics. A lumbar puncture tests the wrong fluid without a meningeal sign, and observation leaves a likely infection untreated
  7. 4-day-old girl has tachycardia and tremor Mother has Graves disease; no maternal drug use Born at 38 weeks poor weight gain since birth exophthalmos warm, moist skin T 37.4 °C · HR 196/min · white blood cells 9,000/mm³ → Neonatal thyrotoxicosis → maternal Graves disease with tachycardia, tremor and exophthalmos; free thyroxine is high and thyroid-stimulating hormone low, and propranolol with methimazole treats it. Sepsis does not explain exophthalmos in the infant of a mother with Graves disease ⚠︎, and neonatal abstinence needs a maternal drug history
  8. 21-day-old boy has fever, irritability and poor feeding bulging anterior fontanelle irritable when handled Born at term; discharged home on day 2; no sick contacts Feeding half his usual volume T 38.8 °C · HR 188/min → Lumbar puncture with blood cultures and empiric ampicillin plus cefotaxime → a previously well infant from home has community-acquired late-onset disease, treated like early-onset disease, and a bulging fontanelle is a meningitis concern: ampicillin covers Listeria, which cephalosporins do not, and cefotaxime replaces gentamicin when meningitis is strongly suspected because it achieves superior cerebrospinal fluid penetration; the lumbar puncture decides whether this is meningitis and so the length of treatment. Ceftriaxone plus vancomycin leaves Listeria uncovered, and observation misses a bulging fontanelle
  9. 7-month-old boy has a rash on his trunk Fever to 39 °C for 3 days ended yesterday blanching rose-pink macules on the trunk playful and well appearing T 37.0 °C · HR 120/min → Roseola infantum → high fever that breaks before a blanching rose-pink truncal rash appears is human herpesvirus 6; no testing is needed. Measles brings the rash with the fever ⚠︎, and a well, playful infant has no meningeal sign
  10. 6-hour-old boy has grunting and nasal flaring Mother had chorioamnionitis during labor Born at 39 weeks after 20 hours of labor; Apgar scores 7 and 8 subcostal retractions HR 170/min · respiratory rate 72/min · oxygen saturation 94% → Blood cultures and empiric ampicillin plus gentamicin → maternal chorioamnionitis with early respiratory distress is early-onset infection until proven otherwise: draw cultures, but do not delay ampicillin with an aminoglycoside. Ceftriaxone plus vancomycin is the right class at the wrong age, and observation delays treatment
  11. 10-month-old boy has fever and irritability bulging anterior fontanelle high-pitched cry Ill for one day, with two episodes of vomiting No rash; no pain-free intervals T 39.3 °C · HR 172/min → Bacterial meningitis → a bulging fontanelle and a high-pitched cry are the infant's meningeal signs, since neck signs are unreliable; neuroimaging only if focal signs are present. Intussusception cries in paroxysms with calm intervals, and roseola brings a rash after the fever
  12. 5-day-old boy was diagnosed with sepsis yesterday Blood culture result pending Born at term; empiric antibiotics are being chosen jaundiced to the chest feeding poorly T 37.9 °C · HR 168/min · total bilirubin 14 mg/dL → Ceftriaxone → ceftriaxone displaces unconjugated bilirubin from albumin (kernicterus risk) and precipitates in the biliary tract as sludge; it is contraindicated in hyperbilirubinemic neonates or with calcium-containing intravenous solutions. Ampicillin and gentamicin are the neonatal regimen
  13. 6-month-old boy has fever and cries whenever he is held bulging anterior fontanelle The lumbar puncture will be delayed an hour T 39.4 °C · HR 176/min · BP 84/50 mm Hg → Give empiric antibiotics now and perform the lumbar puncture after → if the tap is delayed, give antibiotics first: a sterilized Gram stain is an acceptable trade. Waiting, or deferring antibiotics until cultures return, delays treatment ⚠︎
  14. 1-day-old boy born at 39 weeks has grunting and poor feeding Mother had a fever in labor; no intrapartum antibiotics Membranes ruptured 20 hours before delivery lethargic T 38.4 °C · HR 182/min · blood culture pending → Group B Streptococcus → early-onset organisms come from the maternal genital tract, and in a term infant group B Streptococcus leads; intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis prevents early-onset disease. Escherichia coli now predominates among preterm and very low birth weight neonates, and Listeria is the organism ampicillin is kept for
  15. 12-month-old girl has fever and vomiting papilledema on funduscopy; anterior fontanelle closed new weakness of the right arm and leg Empiric intravenous antibiotics have been given T 39.6 °C · HR 168/min · BP 96/58 mm Hg → Head CT before lumbar puncture → papilledema or a focal deficit puts imaging before the tap, and antibiotics come first, then CT, then the lumbar puncture. An immediate tap risks herniation, and magnetic resonance imaging delays the decision without adding to it ⚠︎
  16. 21-day-old girl born at 39 weeks has a fever Well appearing and feeding normally Parents measured the fever an hour ago; no sick contacts no rash, cough or focal findings T 38.4 °C rectal · HR 168/min → Full evaluation including lumbar puncture, admission and empiric antibiotics → at 8 to 21 days the AAP guideline calls for a catheterized urinalysis, a blood culture and cerebrospinal fluid, parenteral antibiotics and hospital monitoring, even when the infant looks well. A urine-only workup or discharge without cerebrospinal fluid falls short in this band
  17. 8-month-old boy has fever, petechiae and lethargy Ill for 12 hours; capillary refill 5 seconds A lumbar puncture tray is being prepared T 39.8 °C · HR 190/min · BP 64/30 mm Hg → Delaying antibiotics to complete the lumbar puncture → treat first, tap after: in shock with petechiae, a lumbar puncture never delays antibiotics. Blood cultures are right as long as they do not delay the first dose, and intravenous fluids treat the shock ⚠︎
Management
Empiric antibiotics by age Neonate (0 to 28 days) – ampicillin plus gentamicin, covering GBS, E. coli and Listeria; cefotaxime may be added to or substituted for the gentamicin if gram-negative meningitis is suspected, and ampicillin plus cefotaxime is preferred when meningitis is strongly suspected or confirmed, for its superior cerebrospinal fluid penetration. The 2021 AAP table lists ampicillin with ceftazidime or gentamicin for 8 to 28 days. Where extended-spectrum beta-lactamase-producing E. coli circulates, gentamicin replaces ceftazidime for suspected bacteremia or sepsis, and meropenem replaces it when meningitis is suspected · 29 to 60 days – ceftriaxone, with vancomycin added when bacteremia or meningitis is a concern; the neonatal organisms recede and ceftriaxone’s biliary risk becomes acceptable · Ceftriaxone in a neonate – avoided: it displaces unconjugated bilirubin from albumin (kernicterus risk) and precipitates in the biliary tract as sludge; contraindicated in hyperbilirubinemic neonates or with calcium-containing intravenous solutions · Herpes simplex virus (HSV) risk – maternal genital HSV lesions or fever 48 hours before or after delivery; vesicles, seizures, hypothermia, mucous membrane ulcers, pleocytosis with a negative Gram stain, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia or raised transaminases: acyclovir joins the parenteral antibiotics
Sequence and its exceptions Head CT precedes the lumbar puncture only for focal deficits, papilledema, altered consciousness or immunocompromise, and then antibiotics precede the CT, not the other way around. In an infant with an open fontanelle the requirement is generally suspended: the fontanelle decompresses rising pressure, so, without a focal deficit or papilledema, tap without imaging first. If the tap will be delayed, give antibiotics first. Draw the blood culture, but never let it delay antibiotics.
8 to 21 days (AAP 2021)
DecisionAction and condition
UrineShould: catheter or suprapubic aspiration specimen for urinalysis, and for culture if the urinalysis is positive
Blood cultureShould obtain
Inflammatory markersMay assess
CSFShould obtain for cell count, protein, glucose, Gram stain and bacterial culture
AntibioticsShould start parenteral therapy
WhereShould actively monitor in hospital, with staff experienced with neonates, while cultures are pending
StopShould stop parenteral antibiotics and discharge when cultures are negative for 24 to 36 hours (or grow only contaminants), the infant still appears well or is improving, and no other reason for hospitalization remains. Should treat a positive culture with targeted therapy for a duration fitting the disease, organism and response
HSVShould be considered with maternal genital HSV lesions or fever from 48 hours before to 48 hours after delivery, or vesicles, seizures, hypothermia, mucous membrane ulcers, pleocytosis without a positive Gram stain, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia or a raised alanine aminotransferase; then parenteral antibiotics including acyclovir
22 to 28 days (AAP 2021)
DecisionAction and condition
UrineShould: catheter or suprapubic specimen for urinalysis and culture if positive, or a bag or voided specimen for urinalysis with a catheter or suprapubic culture if positive
Blood cultureShould obtain
Inflammatory markersShould assess
CSFShould obtain if any marker is abnormal. May obtain even if no marker is abnormal (urinalysis negative or positive), once blood and urine cultures are taken and the infant is hospitalized
Antibiotics, hospitalShould give parenteral therapy if CSF suggests bacterial meningitis or the urinalysis is positive. May give it if CSF and urinalysis are normal but a marker is abnormal, and may even if the urinalysis and all markers are normal and CSF is normal or enterovirus-positive
Antibiotics, homeShould give parenteral therapy before home management, even if the urinalysis, all markers and CSF are normal
HomeMay manage at home if the urinalysis and all markers are normal, CSF is normal or enterovirus-positive, verbal and written instructions are given, a recheck in 24 hours is arranged, and plans for a change in condition (contact with providers, access to emergency care) are in place
HospitalShould admit if CSF is not obtained or is uninterpretable
StopShould stop antibiotics and discharge hospitalized infants after 24 to 36 hours of negative cultures if the infant is well or improving, with no other reason for hospitalization and no other infection needing treatment (such as otitis media). At home, should stop when the infant is well or improving at reassessment, all cultures are negative at 24 to 36 hours and no other infection needs treatment. Should treat a positive culture with targeted therapy for a duration fitting the disease, organism and response
HSVShould be considered (HSV can occur in this age group) with vesicles, seizures, hypothermia, mucous membrane ulcers, pleocytosis without a positive Gram stain, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia or a raised alanine aminotransferase
29 to 60 days (AAP 2021)
DecisionAction and condition
UrineShould: bag or voided specimen for urinalysis with a catheter or suprapubic culture if positive, or a catheter or suprapubic specimen for both
Blood cultureShould obtain
Inflammatory markersShould assess
CSFNeed not obtain if all markers are normal. May obtain if any marker is abnormal, testing for enterovirus when pleocytosis is found or in enterovirus season
AntibioticsShould give parenteral therapy if CSF suggests bacterial meningitis. May give it if CSF (if obtained) is normal and any marker is abnormal. Should start oral therapy if the urinalysis is positive, no marker is abnormal and CSF (if obtained) is normal. Need not give any while cultures are pending if the urinalysis is negative, no marker is abnormal and CSF (if obtained) is normal or enterovirus-positive
HospitalShould admit if CSF (if obtained) is abnormal. May admit if any marker is abnormal
HomeShould manage at home if CSF (if obtained) is normal, the urinalysis is negative and all markers are normal, with parental education, a recheck in 24 hours and plans for a change in condition. May manage at home without antibiotics or interpretable CSF if the urinalysis is negative, all markers are normal and parents can return promptly and agree to follow-up in 24 to 36 hours; reassess within 24 hours
StopShould stop antibiotics when all cultures are negative at 24 to 36 hours, the infant is well or improving and no other infection needs treatment. With a positive urine culture, should discharge if blood and CSF (if obtained) cultures are negative, the infant is well or improving and no other reason for hospitalization remains; at home, should stop parenteral antibiotics (if started) and begin or continue oral therapy when other cultures are negative at 24 to 36 hours and the infant is well or improving. Should treat a positive culture with targeted therapy for a duration fitting the disease, organism and response
HSVShould be considered, although uncommon, with maternal genital HSV lesions or vesicles, seizures, hypothermia, mucous membrane ulcers, pleocytosis without a positive Gram stain, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia or a raised alanine aminotransferase
Organisms and prevention Early-onset organisms come from the maternal genital tract: GBS, E. coli (often carrying the K1 (capsular antigen 1) capsule) and Listeria. Intrapartum penicillin prophylaxis reduced early-onset GBS disease but did not change E. coli rates, and E. coli now predominates among preterm and VLBW neonates. No strategy yet prevents late-onset GBS disease, and its rate is unchanged. GBS remains a leading cause of meningitis and bloodstream infection under 3 months. For GBS disease the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) counts early onset as under 7 days and late onset as 7 to 89 days.
Reading the febrile infant Fever without a source is documented fever with no localizing findings after history and examination. Nuchal rigidity, Kernig and Brudzinski signs are unreliable under roughly 12 to 18 months; look for paradoxical irritability, a bulging fontanelle and a high-pitched cry. A dipstick is a screen, not a rule-out: leukocyte esterase is about 83% sensitive and nitrite about 53%, because infant bladder transit is too short for nitrate reduction; both negative in concentrated urine (specific gravity 1.030) is genuinely reassuring. Loose stools and mild tachypnea are nonspecific systemic responses in a septic infant, not localizing findings. When the sources are eliminated one by one and a meningeal sign remains, do a lumbar puncture. Dexamethasone with or before the first antibiotic dose reduces hearing loss in Haemophilus influenzae type b meningitis. In the first days, 5% weight loss at day 3 is physiologic (up to 7 to 10% in breastfed newborns).
Common wrong answers Neonatal abstinence or hypoglycemia for an irritable, poorly feeding neonate: either fits the behavior, but leukopenia fits neither. Ceftriaxone plus vancomycin under 29 days: the right class of empiric coverage at the wrong age. Propranolol: it treats neonatal thyrotoxicosis, which does not produce leukopenia. Abdominal ultrasound for paradoxical irritability: intussusception is the other inconsolable infant, but its crying is paroxysmal with calm intervals. Urine culture with a meningeal sign: the right class of test on the wrong fluid. Stool testing: three loose stools cannot produce a fever of 39.5 °C with 83% neutrophils.
Pairs with Part I Bacterial Meningitis covers the CSF grid and the neonatal organism-by-host list, so this brief stops at the decision to tap. Ask: am I deciding whether to tap, or reading the fluid? Part I Seizure with Fever in a Child covers what a seizure adds to the decision to tap. Aquifer Fever in an Infant covers which tests the age, appearance and vaccines call for, and the febrile urinary tract infection that is most often found.
Transferable rule

In a neonate the absence of fever does not exclude sepsis: without fever and with no maternal drug history, the WBC decides, not the behavioral pattern. In a febrile infant, name the disease first by elimination, then choose the test that follows from it; each reliable negative finding closes a source, and the diagnosis is the source that remains.
